reading.title: One Latin Root in Motion
reading.purpose: Discover how the Latin root ject connects words about motion, movies, and feelings.
paras: Many English words share a hidden root from Latin. The root ject means "to throw." When you spot ject inside a word, picture something being pushed, tossed, or sent out.

Start with things that fly through the air. A baseball, a paper plane, or an arrow is a projectile, an object thrown or shot forward. The curved path it follows across the sky is called its trajectory. In a movie theater, a projector sends bright light onto a wide screen, so the machine can project clear pictures across a dark room.

The root also shows up in everyday machines and medicine. A toaster will eject warm bread, pushing it out with a pop when it is ready. A nurse can inject liquid medicine through a tiny needle, giving a quick injection that helps protect a patient from illness.

Even feelings and choices borrow this root. If a judge decides to reject a messy entry, the judge refuses to accept it. Hearing a rejection can sting, and a player who loses a close match may feel dejected, sad and low as if their spirits were thrown down.
Learning one root like ject helps you unlock a whole family of useful words.

choices: the curved path of a flying object
a machine that shines light onto a theater screen
a quick shot of liquid medicine from a nurse
the feeling of being sad after losing a match
